title: Trump's Green Card Curbs Test Indian Tech Workers as PERM Freeze Hits Eight Firms
excerpt: Nearly one million Indians are already waiting in the employment-based green card queue. A PERM suspension at Microsoft, Infosys, TCS and five other major employers now freezes the first step of the process for their staff.
body:
• The Trump administration has suspended eight major technology and IT services firms — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini — from the PERM green card sponsorship programme.
  • Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, 79% of all pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.
  • If your employer is one of the eight, a new PERM case cannot start and a pending one is frozen — but your H-1B status and any already-approved green card are not cancelled.
  • Keep proof of your PERM filing and filing date: immigration lawyers say suspended cases keep their dates, which can become your priority date if processing resumes.

For Indian technology workers in the United States, the path to a green card has narrowed again. The Trump administration's suspension of eight major employers from the PERM labour certification programme — the first, mandatory step in most employer-sponsored green card cases — has left thousands of workers unsure whether the permanent residency they have waited years for will move at all, according to a BBC report on the curbs and their fallout.

The companies affected are Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini. Under the suspension, announced on October 8, the firms cannot file new PERM applications and processing of their pending applications is halted while federal investigations into alleged misuse of employment-based immigration programmes continue. US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling has linked the action to ongoing federal and criminal investigations; a suspension, by itself, does not establish wrongdoing by any company.

What PERM Is, and Why Freezing It Matters

PERM — formally, Permanent Labor Certification — is the stage at which an employer must show the Department of Labor that no qualified US worker is available for the job and that hiring the foreign worker will not hurt the wages or conditions of American workers doing similar work. Only after PERM is certified can the employer file the I-140 immigrant petition that places a worker in the green card queue. The Department of Labor explains the process on its PERM programme page, and USCIS sets out the next step on its I-140 petition page.

The freeze lands on a queue that was already the longest in the system. Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025 — 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Its analysis projects wait times of five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing from January 2026, depending on the category, a consequence of the per-country cap that limits any one country to 7% of employment-based green cards each year.

What the Suspension Does Not Do

Immigration specialists have been quick to draw a line between the PERM freeze and workers' current status. The action does not cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards that have already been approved, immigration specialist Swatilina Barik noted in a widely shared assessment reported by The American Bazaar. It restricts the permanent-residency pathway through the eight employers; it does not end temporary work authorisation.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon."

— Indian technology professional in the US, speaking to the BBC on condition of anonymity

Workers whose PERM has already been certified are in a different position from those still waiting: lawyers advising affected employees say pending applications are frozen, not rejected, and retain their filing dates. The practical risk is sharpest for workers approaching the six-year H-1B limit who have not yet progressed far enough in the green card process to qualify for extensions beyond it.

The Alternatives Workers Are Weighing

Some workers are looking at routes that bypass PERM altogether. Categories for individuals with extraordinary ability and for work in the national interest do not require labour certification, though advisers quoted in coverage of the freeze warn those categories may face scrutiny next. Others are considering the EB-5 investor route, which requires an investment of at least $800,000 in an eligible US enterprise — a sum many salaried professionals do not have.

There is also a corporate response taking shape. Industry executives say restrictions are already pushing more work offshore to India, where companies capture cost savings and, since the pandemic, face fewer client objections to remote delivery. Research cited in the BBC report suggests curbs may shift jobs to India rather than to American workers.

What Happens Next

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. It follows a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions that was later struck down by federal courts, and a more recent proposal for a $70,000 fee tied to universities recommending international students for post-study work. For the roughly 70% of H-1B holders who are Indian nationals, the immediate task is unglamorous but essential: confirm which stage your case is at, keep every filing receipt, and do not assume any deadline has moved.
